title: Slices Holding a, b and c
statement:
You get a string s made only of the letters a, b and c.

Count the contiguous substrings of s that contain each of the three letters at least once. Substrings at different positions count separately, even if they read the same.

examples.why: Only the whole string has all three letters.
"aabc" and "abc". Both end at the c, but they start at different places.

hints: Fix where a substring ends. Which starting positions make it contain all three letters?
If the substring s[i..r] contains all three letters, so does every substring that starts further left and ends at r.
Remember the last position where you saw each letter. For the end r, any start up to the smallest of those three positions works, which is min(last) + 1 starts.

explain.intuition:
Counting substrings one by one is quadratic. Instead, count them by their right end. For a fixed end r, a start works exactly when the substring still reaches back to the most recent a, the most recent b and the most recent c. The binding one is the oldest of the three.

So if last holds the latest index of each letter, the valid starts are 0..min(last), which is min(last) + 1 substrings. Add that for every r. Until all three letters have appeared, the minimum is −1 and the term is 0. This is a sliding window where the left edge is computed rather than moved step by step.
pitfalls: Counting only the shortest valid window per end. Every longer extension to the left also counts.
Counting distinct strings instead of positions. In "abcabc" the slice "abc" counts once per place it occurs.
Using a 32-bit counter in languages that have one. With 50 000 letters the answer can exceed a billion.

solutions.title: Extend from every start
solutions.idea: For each start, walk right until all three letters have been seen. Every longer substring from that start also qualifies.

solutions.title: Last-seen positions
solutions.idea: For each end r, the number of valid starts is one more than the oldest of the three last-seen positions.

followups: Count the substrings that contain at most two distinct letters instead.
Generalise to an alphabet of k letters where every letter must appear. How does the cost per step change?
lcTitle: Number of Substrings Containing All Three Characters
